topic: Will France's crisis put the welfare-state model in question?
title_options: Can France Still Afford Its Welfare State?
Why France Can't Stop Protesting (And Can't Stop Borrowing)
Is Europe's Most Generous Welfare State Breaking?
description:
France's streets are full again. More than half a million people marched on 17 October 2026 as school protests merged with anger over a €54 billion austerity budget. Behind it is a bigger question: can France still afford the most generous welfare state in Europe, and is the model itself breaking?

We look at the numbers: public spending, pensions, debt, demography, and how Denmark and Sweden run big welfare states without big deficits.

scenes.narration: On October 17, about 550,000 people marched across France, according to the Interior Ministry. By nightfall, 1,200 had been arrested.
In Limoges, a fire largely destroyed the historic town hall.
It started with teenagers. Last month, high school students in the working-class suburbs north of Paris walked out over missing teachers and crumbling classrooms.
Within weeks, it had spread to Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Lille and Marseille, and merged with a public sector strike against the government's budget.
Because the budget for 2027 asks for 54 billion euros in savings and new taxes.
And that raises a bigger question than one budget. Can France still afford the welfare state it is famous for? Or is the model itself starting to crack?
In 2025, French public spending reached 57.2 percent of everything the economy produced. That is about seven points more than the euro area average.

chart.title: Public spending, % of GDP, 2025
chart.source: INSEE; euro-area gap per Kyiv Post / Eurostat

scenes.narration: Just over 30 percent of GDP goes on social spending alone: pensions, health, families and unemployment. In the OECD, only Austria and Finland are in the same league.
In return, the French get a lot. Health care that is cheap at the point of use. Strong protection for workers. And some of the most generous pensions in the world.
A French pension replaces about 72 percent of a worker's earnings, compared with around 55 percent in Germany and 50 percent in the United States.

chart.title: Pension as % of previous earnings
chart.source: OECD net replacement rates, via Kyiv Post

scenes.narration: Pensions alone cost around 14 percent of GDP, among the highest in the developed world, according to the OECD.
This is the French social model. Built after the Second World War, it is paid for mostly by contributions taken from wages. Today's workers pay for today's retirees.
But the money going out has been bigger than the money coming in for a very long time. France has not run a budget surplus since 1974.
In 2025, the deficit was 5.1 percent of GDP, far above the 3 percent limit in the European Union's rules.
And every deficit adds to the debt. By the end of 2025, it reached 115.6 percent of GDP.
That is the third highest in the euro zone, behind only Greece and Italy, and almost twice Germany's level.
And debt is no longer cheap. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says rising interest rates and tension abroad add another 10 billion euros to next year's bill.
In his words: we can no longer finance everything.
Every attempt to trim the model has met the street. In 2019, a plan to overhaul pensions brought weeks of strikes and marches.
In 2018, a rise in fuel tax sparked the yellow vest movement, which lasted for months.
In 2023, President Macron raised the retirement age from 62 to 64, pushing it through without a final vote in parliament.
Then the 2024 snap election produced a hung parliament. No bloc has a majority.
Two governments have fallen over budgets since: Michel Barnier's in December 2024, and François Bayrou's in September 2025.
To survive, Lecornu's government suspended the pension reform until after the 2027 presidential election. That costs 400 million euros next year, and 1.8 billion the year after.
Behind the politics is a slower problem. In 2024, France had 2.5 people of working age for every person over 65. By 2070, the projection is 1.76.
In a system where workers pay for retirees, that ratio is the whole equation. Fewer workers per retiree means higher contributions, lower pensions, or later retirement. Every option hurts someone.
And the cuts have to land somewhere. The 2027 budget freezes civil servants' pay scale, for the fourth year in a row according to unions, and freezes all but the lowest pensions.
Teachers, nurses and students feel it first. That is exactly what the teenagers marched about: overcrowded classes, missing teachers, ageing schools.
But here is what most people get wrong. A big welfare state is not the problem on its own. Denmark and Sweden also tax and spend heavily.
Yet in 2025, Denmark ran a budget surplus, and Sweden's debt was just 35 percent of GDP.
The difference is not generosity. Sweden's pensions adjust automatically to keep the system in balance, and Denmark links its retirement age to life expectancy.

France has kept the benefits, but not the balance. Its taxes are already among the highest in Europe, at 43.6 percent of GDP. Raising them is toxic, and cutting benefits brings people onto the streets. So the gap is filled by borrowing.
The presidential election is due in April 2027, and Marine Le Pen's National Rally, which has promised to undo the pension reform, is strong in the polls.
So, is the French welfare model finished? Not quite. Its promise is still hugely popular, and richer countries pay for similar ones.
But the numbers say this version cannot last unchanged. The only question is who decides how it changes: parliament, the bond markets, or the street.
Whoever wins in 2027 will have to answer the question the students are asking right now. Who pays for the French model?
